typeName: Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results, with Graphing
title: Heat and leakage from beet cells

stimulus.title: Heat and leakage from beet cells
stimulus.html:
Beet root cells store a red, water-soluble substance in a large central vacuole surrounded by a membrane, inside a cell enclosed by the plasma membrane. Researchers cut 24 identical cubes from one beet and rinsed them. They heated groups of six cubes for 1 minute in water baths at 30, 45, 60 or 75 °C, then placed each cube in 10 mL of distilled water at room temperature for 20 minutes. They measured how red the water became as absorbance (higher absorbance means more of the red substance in the water).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Explain why little of the red substance leaves an undamaged beet cell.

rubric.point: The substance is polar or charged (water-soluble), so it cannot cross the hydrophobic interior of the phospholipid bilayer (and there are no transport proteins letting it out).
accept: the hydrophobic core of the membrane blocks water-soluble molecules
membranes are selectively permeable and the polar substance cannot diffuse through the nonpolar tails
the bilayer keeps large polar molecules inside the vacuole and cell

parts.sample: The red substance is water-soluble (polar), and the inside of the membrane is made of the nonpolar fatty acid tails of phospholipids. Polar molecules cannot pass through that hydrophobic layer, so an intact, selectively permeable membrane keeps the substance inside the vacuole and the cell.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: (i) Identify the independent variable in the experiment. (ii) The researchers treated the 30 °C group as a control. Justify this choice by stating what it allows them to rule out.

rubric.point: (i) The temperature at which the cubes were heated.

(ii) 30 °C is close to normal conditions that do not damage membranes, so it shows how much red substance leaks from cut cells without heat damage (from cells cut open while preparing the cubes); it rules out that leakage at higher temperatures comes from cutting, handling or soaking alone.
accept: baseline leakage from cut surfaces and handling
shows leakage without heat damage so the extra leakage can be credited to heat
rules out that the soaking or cutting caused the color

parts.sample: (i) The heating temperature. (ii) At 30 °C the membranes are not heat-damaged, so this group shows the baseline leakage caused by cutting the cubes (which opens some cells), rinsing and soaking. Comparing other groups with it rules out that their extra color came from the procedure rather than from the higher temperature.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Construct an appropriately labeled graph that shows the mean absorbance at each temperature, with error bars showing the 95% confidence interval (mean ± 2SE).

rubric.point: Correct orientation and labels: heating temperature (°C) on the x-axis, absorbance (arbitrary units) on the y-axis, each axis labeled with the quantity and units.
accept: x: Temperature (°C); y: Absorbance (arbitrary units or AU)

rubric.point: Appropriate, evenly spaced scales that use most of the grid (for example y from 0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1 or 0.2; x from 0 or 30 to 75 in even steps, or four evenly spaced categories for a bar graph).
accept: axis may start above zero if labeled

rubric.point: All four means plotted correctly (0.10, 0.16, 0.52, 0.81) as points (line graph or scatterplot, connected or not) or as bars.
accept: line graph of the four means
bar graph with one bar per temperature

parts.sample: A line graph with x-axis "Heating temperature (°C)" from 0 to 80 in steps of 10 and y-axis "Absorbance (arbitrary units)" from 0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1. Points at (30, 0.10), (45, 0.16), (60, 0.52) and (75, 0.81), joined by straight lines. Error bars from 0.06 to 0.14 at 30 °C, 0.10 to 0.22 at 45 °C, 0.44 to 0.60 at 60 °C and 0.71 to 0.91 at 75 °C. Caption: "Error bars show 95% confidence intervals (mean ± 2SE)."

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: (i) Based on your graph, determine whether heating to 45 °C caused more leakage than heating to 30 °C, and justify your answer. (ii) Explain the large increase in leakage between 45 °C and 75 °C in terms of membrane structure.

rubric.point: (i) No difference is shown: the 95% CIs for 30 °C (0.06-0.14) and 45 °C (0.10-0.22) overlap, so the difference is not statistically significant (fail to reject the null hypothesis).
accept: error bars overlap so the data do not show that 45 °C caused more leakage
cannot conclude a difference because the confidence intervals overlap

rubric.point: (ii) High temperature disrupts the membrane: proteins in the membrane denature (unfold) and the bilayer becomes much more fluid or disorganized, creating gaps, so the polar red substance escapes.
accept: heat denatures membrane proteins, leaving holes
phospholipids move apart as fluidity increases, so the membrane loses its selective permeability

parts.sample: (i) No. The 95% confidence intervals overlap (0.06-0.14 at 30 °C and 0.10-0.22 at 45 °C), so the data do not show a significant difference; we fail to reject the null hypothesis that these temperatures cause the same leakage. (ii) Above about 45 °C, heat denatures the proteins embedded in the membranes and makes the phospholipid bilayer far more fluid, so gaps open and the membranes stop being selectively permeable. The water-soluble red substance then leaks out of the vacuole and the cell, raising absorbance.

graphSpec.alsoAccepted: a bar graph with one bar per temperature and the same error bars
